text: The index-pairing trick from the last lesson makes simulating a gate cheap, but it can't rescue the one thing that's fundamentally expensive: the state vector itself has 2 to the n entries, and that number explodes far faster than any amount of hardware improvement can keep up with. This is the single most important practical fact separating simulating quantum computing from doing quantum computing.

Each amplitude costs 16 bytes, two 8-byte doubles, so an n-qubit state vector needs 2 to the n times 16 bytes. 24 qubits is 256 megabytes, comfortable on a laptop. 30 qubits is 16 gigabytes, right at the edge of a high-end machine. 40 qubits is 16 terabytes, roughly the ceiling for the world's largest supercomputers today. 50 qubits is 16 petabytes, already past what any single facility stores for this purpose — and every additional qubit doubles the requirement again.

This isn't a software inefficiency a cleverer simulator could fix. It's a direct consequence of what an n-qubit state actually is: a point in a 2 to the n dimensional vector space, full stop. The previous lesson's index-pairing trick makes applying each gate efficient, but it can't shrink the vector itself, because every one of those amplitudes can, in general, be nonzero and physically meaningful at once. There's no way to represent a general n-qubit state in fewer than roughly 2 to the n numbers.

This is exactly the resource gap that makes quantum hardware interesting. A real quantum computer with n physical qubits doesn't need to store 2 to the n numbers anywhere — it simply is in that superposition, as a direct physical fact about n physical objects, with no memory cost growing beyond the n qubits themselves. What hardware doesn't get for free is reading that state out usefully — measurement still only yields n classical bits per run, same as Chapter 1 established.

Next lesson covers everything else real hardware gives up compared to a noiseless simulator: gate errors, one-time measurement instead of reading exact probabilities, and a fixed, limited connectivity between physical qubits.
